blocks.text: 1. Pooling

blocks.alt: A feature map gets downsampled through pooling

blocks.text: Stride, the previous topic, showed that skipping positions can act similarly to downsampling. Pooling is a dedicated technique for deliberately reducing spatial resolution, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
It works by summarizing a small local region into a single representative value, a genuinely distinct, standalone operation covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Connection To Stride
This connects back to stride as a form of downsampling, already covered in the previous topic. Pooling shares that same underlying goal, but as its own genuinely dedicated technique.
It exists rather than a side effect of the convolution's own stride setting, already covered, giving networks a genuinely separate, dedicated tool for deliberately reducing spatial resolution.
3. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: A small window gets reduced to a single value

blocks.text: Pooling's genuinely core idea slides a small window across a feature map, already covered in the Convolution Operation, examining local regions one at a time, similar in structure to that earlier operation.
At each position, it summarizes that region into a single output value, the exact summarization rule depending on the specific pooling variant, covered further in the next two sections.

blocks.text: 4. A Preview Of Max Pooling

blocks.alt: A window keeps the max value

blocks.text: A genuinely common pooling variant, covered in full in the next topic, takes the genuinely largest value within each small window, rather than any other summary statistic.
This is called Max Pooling, keeping only the genuinely strongest signal in each local region, a genuinely intuitive approach explored in complete depth in the very next topic of this module.
5. A Preview Of Average Pooling

blocks.alt: A window keeps the average value

blocks.text: Another genuinely common pooling variant, covered further later in this module, takes the genuinely average value within each small window instead of the maximum already covered in the previous section.
This is called Average Pooling, smoothing the local region rather than keeping just its peak, a genuinely different summarization philosophy explored in complete depth later in this module.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Max Pooling and Average Pooling, both previewed in this topic, are the two most common pooling variants in practice, each covered in its own complete, dedicated topic immediately following this one.

blocks.text: 6. No Learnable Parameters

blocks.alt: Pooling has no weights to learn

blocks.text: This connects back to filters, already covered as learnable weights in Filters and Kernels. Pooling genuinely has no learnable parameters of its own, a genuinely important structural difference from convolutional layers.
It is a genuinely fixed, deterministic operation, unlike the convolution it commonly follows, since the pooling rule, already covered in the previous two sections, never changes during training.
7. Why Reducing Spatial Size Genuinely Matters

A genuinely important motivating benefit connects back to computational efficiency, already covered in Stride. A genuinely smaller feature map means genuinely less computation for every subsequent layer that processes it.

This compounds across a genuinely deep network, already covered in Network Architecture, where the savings from each pooling layer, already covered in this topic, benefit every layer that comes afterward.
8. Strengthening Translation Invariance

blocks.alt: Pooling makes the network more robust to small shifts

blocks.text: This connects back to translation invariance, already covered in the Convolution Operation. Pooling genuinely strengthens this same property even further, beyond what parameter sharing alone already provided.

A small shift in the input often produces the exact same pooled output, since summarizing a small region into one value, already covered in this topic, genuinely absorbs minor positional shifts within that region.

blocks.text: 9. A Mild Regularizing Effect

This connects back to Overfitting, already covered in its own topic. Fewer parameters overall, already covered as no learnable parameters in this topic, genuinely helps reduce the risk of overfitting.

This is a mild but genuinely real regularizing effect, a welcome side benefit rather than pooling's own primary purpose, which remains the spatial reduction already covered throughout most of this topic.
10. Recognizing Why Pooling Is Genuinely A Standard Component

This connects back to typical Convolutional Neural Network architectures, covered further in CNN Architectures. Pooling layers, already covered, commonly appear between convolutional layers throughout these designs.
Wanting genuinely stronger translation invariance and reduced computation together is another genuine case where Pooling, already covered, directly delivers both benefits at once.
11. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simple pooling operation, sliding a 2x2 window across a feature map and summarizing each region, illustrating the core mechanism already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

feature_map = np.array([
    [1, 3, 2, 4],
    [5, 6, 1, 2],
    [7, 2, 9, 4],
    [3, 1, 0, 8],
])

pool_size = 2
stride = 2  # already covered in the previous topic, commonly matching the pool size

output_size = (feature_map.shape[0] - pool_size) // stride + 1
pooled_output = np.zeros((output_size, output_size))

for i in range(output_size):
    for j in range(output_size):
        row, col = i * stride, j * stride
        region = feature_map[row:row + pool_size, col:col + pool_size]
        pooled_output[i, j] = region.max()  # this specific choice is already covered as Max Pooling in this topic

print("Original feature map shape:", feature_map.shape)
print("Pooled output shape (genuinely smaller, already covered in this topic):", pooled_output.shape)
print("Pooled output:\n", pooled_output)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the feature map shrinking from 4x4 to 2x2, exactly the deliberate spatial reduction already covered as this topic's own core purpose, using the maximum value from each 2x2 region.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Pooling summarizes a small local region of a feature map into a single output value.
It is a dedicated technique for deliberately reducing spatial resolution.
Max Pooling and Average Pooling are the two most common pooling variants, each covered separately.
Pooling has no learnable parameters, unlike the convolution it commonly follows.
Reducing spatial size cuts computation for every subsequent layer that processes the feature map.
Pooling strengthens translation invariance beyond what parameter sharing alone provides.
Fewer overall parameters gives pooling a mild, real regularizing effect against overfitting.
Pooling layers commonly appear between convolutional layers throughout typical architectures.
